ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Medication-associated sinus suppression

A patient develops fatigue and a new junctional escape rhythm after a beta-blocker dose increase. There are no ischemic symptoms and electrolytes are normal. Which mechanism most plausibly explains the change in pacemaker dominance?

  1. Suppression of sinus-node automaticity allowing a junctional focus to escape
  2. Selective acceleration of the sinus node above the junctional rate
  3. Creation of a new accessory pathway within hours
  4. Permanent destruction of both bundle branches
  5. Direct generation of atrial flutter by every beta blocker
Answer and explanation

Suppression of sinus-node automaticity allowing a junctional focus to escape

Rate-slowing medication can suppress the normal dominant pacemaker enough for a subsidiary focus to emerge.

Option explanations

Suppression of sinus-node automaticity allowing a junctional focus to escape: Rate-slowing medication can suppress the normal dominant pacemaker enough for a subsidiary focus to emerge.

Selective acceleration of the sinus node above the junctional rate: Acceleration of the sinus node would tend to preserve sinus dominance.

Creation of a new accessory pathway within hours: A medication dose change does not create a new anatomic pathway.

Permanent destruction of both bundle branches: The tracing does not imply bilateral bundle destruction.

Direct generation of atrial flutter by every beta blocker: Beta blockers do not universally induce flutter.
